lessons.title: Type juggling: loose == vs strict ===
lessons.summary: The two comparison operators answer different questions. This lesson rebuilds the falsy table, the PHP 8 numeric-string change and the famous null/'0'/'' asymmetry from first principles — so you can predict == results instead of memorising a matrix.

payload.text: Interviewers love loose-vs-strict questions not because `==` is exotic, but because real codebases ship silent bugs when an id, a flag or an input that can legitimately be `0`, `'0'`, `''`, `null` or `false` is compared loosely. If you can explain **why** each result happens, you can answer any variant on the spot. The two quiz questions in this module test exactly this.

sections.title: What the two operators actually ask

payload.text:
`===` (strict) asks: *same value **and** same type?* It never converts anything — an `int` and a `string` can never be `===`.

`==` (loose) asks: *same value after coercing one side to the other's type?* The coercion rules depend on the operand types, and they contain asymmetries that look like bugs. The practical rule most senior codebases follow: **use `===` by default and reach for `==` only when you deliberately want a numeric string (`'007'`, `'1e3'`) to be treated as a number.**

sections.title: The 'empty-ish' values and their web of == relations

payload.text: The dangerous cluster is the group of values that all *feel* empty. Each column below was verified on PHP 8. `== null` and `== 0` are NOT the same test:

payload.title: Four empty-ish values under loose comparison (PHP 8)
payload.note: Rows marked **bold** are the traps: `'0'` is falsy yet NOT `== null`, and `''` is `== null` but NOT `== 0` on PHP 8.

payload.text: If you test user input or a lookup result with `if ($value == null)` you silently **miss the string `'0'`** — a perfectly plausible value (a zero id, a 'no' flag). `filter_input()` and query params routinely hand you `''`, `null`, `'0'` and `false` for the same logical field. Handle them explicitly: `if ($value === null || $value === '')`.
payload.title: `== null` is not an 'is empty' check

steps.title: Start: `0 == '0'`
steps.text: Left side is `int 0`, right side is the string `'0'`. Loose comparison between a number and a **numeric string** converts the string to a number first.

steps.title: Both sides are now ints
steps.text: `'0'` coerces to `0`, so the expression becomes `0 == 0`.

steps.title: Verdict for `==`
steps.text: Equal values, equal ints → `true`.

steps.title: Now `0 === '0'`
steps.text: Strict comparison checks the **type** before anything else: `int` vs `string`. Types differ, so the answer is `false` without any value conversion.

sections.title: What PHP 8 changed in string-vs-number comparisons

payload.text: Before PHP 8, a **non-numeric** string compared loosely to a number was treated as `0` — so `0 == 'abc'` was `true`, a legendary source of bugs. Since PHP 8, only **numeric strings** coerce to numbers; any other string stays a string and the number is converted to a string for the comparison instead.

payload.title: Before vs after (same code, different results)
rows: 'abc' is not numeric → compared as string '0' vs 'abc'
'0' is a numeric string → coerces to int 0
hex strings stopped being numeric in PHP 8

payload.html:
null↓true
0  int↓true
''↓true
'0'↓false
false↓true
payload.title: The asymmetry at a glance: what is loosely equal to null
payload.caption: `'0'` is the only falsy value in the group that is NOT loosely equal to null — `'' == null` is true, `'0' == null` is false.

payload.text: Write comparisons against a **known type**: validate/convert input first (the module's `safe_int` task exists for this), then use `===`. When you genuinely must accept several representations, enumerate them: `in_array($v, [null, '', '0'], true)`. Never write `== null`, `== 0`, `== false` or `== ''` as 'is empty' checks.
payload.title: Compare like a type system, not like a truth table

payload.text: Want the feeling of the trap in code? Try the `safe_int` drill in this module — it is the production-grade answer to '(int) $anything', and the debug sibling shows exactly how a loose cast eats `'abc'` or `null`.

lessons.title: Regex in PHP without the guesswork
lessons.summary: preg_match does not return a boolean. Learn the 1 / 0 / false contract, how $matches is shaped by capture groups, and when to reach for preg_match_all, preg_replace or plain str_contains instead.

payload.text: The quiz question 'what does `preg_match` return' is a filter question: people who used `if (preg_match(...))` their whole career usually cannot answer it precisely. Once the return contract and the `$matches` layout are automatic, regex tasks like `extract_emails` and `normalize_phone` stop being guesswork.

steps.title: Pattern matched
steps.text: Returns the **integer 1**, stops after the first match, fills `$matches[0]` with the whole matched substring.

steps.title: No match found
steps.text: Returns the **integer 0**; `$matches` is untouched (or emptied).

steps.title: Pattern is invalid
steps.text: Returns **`false`** and raises a warning — e.g. an unterminated group or character class.

payload.intro: Three outcomes, three distinct values. This is why truthiness tests hide bugs:

payload.title: The three return values

payload.text: `1 == true` and `0 == true` are both fine, but `false == true` is also fine — so `if (preg_match(...) == true)` can never detect the **pattern-error** case. Branch on the exact value: `=== 1` matched, `=== 0` no match, `=== false` bad pattern.
payload.title: Check === 1 / === 0 / === false

payload.text: `$matches[0]` is always the **full** match. Parenthesised groups follow as `[1]`, `[2]`, … in left-to-right order; named groups `(?P<name>...)` are also exposed under their name. Two traps: a group that did not participate is an empty string, and the match does **not** have to start at position 0 — the engine finds the earliest position where the whole pattern matches.

payload.title: Group layout — and why the first one skips 'jan.'

payload.text: The first pattern cannot match `jan` because `\w` does not include the dot, and the engine will not start the match in the middle of what could be a full match — it starts as early as possible, which is at `kowalski`. If you want the whole address, anchor with `^...$` and use `[^@]+` (anything but `@`) as the task solutions do.

payload.title: Choosing between the string/regex tools
rows: preg_* for patterns, str_* for literals

sections.title: Validate, don't search — anchors change everything

steps.title: The shape check first
steps.text: `'/^[0-9]{9}$/'` means: nine digits **and nothing else** — the `^` and `$` anchors pin the pattern to the whole string. Without anchors, `preg_match('/[0-9]{9}/', 'x600123456y')` returns 1 (it finds nine digits *inside*).

steps.title: Normalise before validating
steps.text: Real phone input contains spaces, dashes and parentheses. Strip them with a character class `'/[\s\-().]/'` first, then run the anchored shape check. That two-stage order (clean → validate) is the entire `normalize_phone` task.

steps.title: Reject, don't coerce
steps.text: For identifiers, return `false`/`null` when the shape does not match — never try to 'fix' it by casting. Digits that fail the format are data errors, not numbers to salvage.

steps.title: preg_match_all fills an array of arrays
steps.text: `$matches[0]` holds **all** full matches; each capture group gets its own array under `[1]`, `[2]`, …. That is why email extraction uses it instead of a `preg_match` loop.

steps.title: Deduplicate with strict in_array
steps.text: `preg_match_all` happily reports duplicates. Keep a `$seen` list and append only addresses not already present — using `in_array(..., true)` so `'0'`-style strings are never confused.

payload.text: A pattern is a quoted string: `/pattern/` — the first unescaped `/` **ends** the delimiter, so a literal slash inside must be escaped (`\/`) or you switch delimiter (`'#https?://#'`). To match a metacharacter literally (`. * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | ^ $ \`), escape it, or build the literal part with `preg_quote($string, '/')`. When in doubt: `preg_quote` first, regex second.
payload.title: The boring 20% that causes most pattern errors

lessons.title: String pipelines: slugify, phone numbers, masking
lessons.summary: Most plain-PHP string tasks are transformation pipelines: several small stages applied in the right order. Learn why transliteration must use strtr, then walk slugify and phone normalisation stage by stage, watching the string change state.

payload.text: Slugify, phone normalisation and masking look unrelated, but they share one skeleton: **input → stage 1 → stage 2 → … → output**, where every stage is a single, testable transformation. Solve them by deciding the stage order first, then writing one line per stage — and verify the string's state after each stage, exactly like the step tables below.

sections.title: strtr vs str_replace: single pass vs sequential

payload.text: `str_replace` applies its replacements **sequentially to the result**, so a later rule can re-translate what an earlier rule just produced. `strtr($s, $map)` with an associative array scans each character **once** (longest keys first) and never re-reads its own output. Transliteration **must** be single-pass — that is the whole point of the strtr quiz question.

payload.title: One input, two outcomes
rows: the fresh `a` is NOT touched again

payload.text: Your transliteration map maps `ż → z` and also handles other letters. If you used `str_replace` with two arrays, a later rule that touches `z` (or a second pass that lowercases and re-applies) would silently rewrite your freshly produced `z`. `strtr` guarantees each input character is translated exactly once.
payload.title: Already-replaced output gets re-replaced

sections.title: The slugify pipeline, stage by stage

payload.html:
'Zażółć gęślą jaźń!'raw title→
strtr($map)transliterate→
strtolowerlowercase→
preg_replacecollapse junk→
trim('-')edges→
'zasolc-gesla-jazn'slug
payload.title: Four stages, one purpose each

steps.title: Stage 1 — transliterate
steps.text: `strtr($title, $map)` replaces Polish letters with ASCII equivalents in one single pass (`ż→z`, `ź→z`, `ą→a`, …). Every non-ASCII character must have an entry, including uppercase ones.

steps.title: Stage 2 — lowercase
steps.text: `strtolower()` — by now the string is pure ASCII, so byte-wise lowercasing is safe (no `mb_strtolower` needed in the dojo sandbox).

steps.title: Stage 3 — collapse junk to one separator
steps.text: `preg_replace('/[^a-z0-9]+/', '-', ...)` turns any run of 'not a lowercase letter or digit' — spaces, punctuation, multiple separators — into a single dash. The `+` is what merges `' -  '` into one dash.

steps.title: Stage 4 — trim the edges
steps.text: Input that starts or ends with junk leaves a leading/trailing dash (see the state above). `trim($slug, '-')` removes only edge dashes — this is exactly what the *'slugify leaves leading/trailing dashes'* debug task plants a bug in.

payload.title: slugify('Zażółć gęślą jaźń!')
payload.intro: Each stage is one line. Watch the state column — if a stage does not produce the shown state, that stage (not the next one) has the bug.

payload.title: Reference implementation

steps.title: Strip all separators
steps.text: `preg_replace('/[\s\-().]/', '', $phone)` removes spaces, dashes, dots and parentheses in one pass (a character class, not three `str_replace` calls). The debug variant that only strips spaces fails here.

steps.title: Remove the country prefix
steps.text: Strip `+48` (3 chars), or `0048` (4 chars), or a bare `48` only when the remainder is 9 digits — check `str_starts_with` in that exact order.

steps.title: Shape-check with anchors
steps.text: `'/^[0-9]{9}$/'` — exactly nine digits. Anything else returns `null` (the 'reject, don't coerce' rule from the regex lesson).

sections.title: Masking: locate the structure, then rebuild

payload.text: `mask_email` is the least 'pipeline' of the three but the same discipline applies: find the structural point (`strpos($email, '@')`), split the string, transform the part you must hide, and concatenate. Byte-string operations (`substr`, `strlen`, `str_repeat`) are all you need for ASCII emails.

payload.title: Mask the middle of the local part

payload.text: Every string task in this module has planted edge cases: empty input, `''` (should return `''`, not `null`), a 1-2 character local part (should not crash on `$local[$len-1]`), a missing `@` (return the input unchanged). When an interviewer asks 'what else do you test?', rattle these off — it is half the score.
payload.title: Empty strings and short inputs are the hidden tests

lessons.title: Bytes and hex: encoding strings the way PHP sees them
lessons.summary: hex conversion is byte-level: every byte (0–255) becomes exactly two hex digits. Learn to reason about strings as byte arrays, and why the naive dechex loop drops the leading zero.

payload.text: The two hex tasks look trivial — and then the debug variants fail half the people who try them. The reason is almost always the same: thinking of a string as 'characters' instead of as a sequence of bytes. This lesson makes the byte view automatic.

sections.title: A string is an array of bytes

payload.text: Every PHP string is a byte sequence. A byte holds 0–255, and hex writes it as exactly **two** digits: `0x0A` → `'0a'`, `0x41` → `'41'`, `0xFF` → `'ff'`. Encoding to hex means: for each byte, emit its two-digit lowercase hex. Decoding is the inverse: pair up digits, each pair becomes one byte.

steps.title: Take the bytes
steps.text: `'A1!'` is the three bytes `0x41`, `0x31`, `0x21` — nothing more.

steps.title: Result
steps.text: `bin2hex('A1!')` gives exactly this — it is the whole solution.

payload.title: The reference solution is one line

steps.title: The dechex trap
steps.text: A hand-rolled loop with `dechex(ord($s[$i]))` produces **one** digit for bytes under 16: `chr(10)` → `dechex(10)` → `'a'` instead of `'0a'`. The output silently changes length.

steps.title: Why padding matters
steps.text: Hex pairs are the unit of decoding. If an encoder ever emits a single digit, the stream is no longer parseable — the next decoder pairs digits from the wrong position. This is the planted bug in the *'str_to_hex loses the leading zero'* debug task.

steps.title: The fix
steps.text: Never hand-roll the loop. Use `bin2hex()`; if you must format manually, pad: `sprintf('%02x', ord($byte))`.

payload.title: The leading-zero bug, step by step

steps.title: hex2bin pairs the digits
steps.text: `hex2bin('616263')` → `'abc'`. One pair, one byte.

steps.title: Malformed input fails loudly
steps.text: Odd length (`'6'`) or non-hex characters (`'zz'`) make `hex2bin` return **`false`** with a warning. An empty string decodes to `''` cleanly — but only if you did not pre-check with a pattern that rejects empty.

steps.title: Validate before you decode
steps.text: Check `/^[0-9a-f]*$/` and an even length first, then decode; treat `false` as invalid input, never as a value. Note the asymmetry: `bin2hex('') === ''` (empty is a valid encoding).

payload.text: The *'hex_to_str returns null for the empty string'* debug task plants exactly this: a guard like `if ($s === '') return null;` is wrong, because `''` is a perfectly valid hex string that should decode to `''`. Only genuinely malformed input (odd length, non-hex) deserves `null`.
payload.title: '' is valid hex

payload.text: Interview echo: when they ask 'how do you store binary in a text column / URL?', the answer starts with 'encode each byte as two hex digits…' — and the pad rule is the detail that separates people who have shipped it from people who read about it.

lessons.title: Checksum validators: Luhn, ISBN, PESEL, NIP
lessons.summary: Four real-world validators, one recipe: sanitise → shape-check → weighted sum → compare the check digit. Walk Luhn, ISBN-10/13, PESEL and NIP digit by digit with the running totals, so the algorithms become something you can rebuild, not recite.

payload.text: The dojo has six checksum tasks (ISBN-10, ISBN-13, ISBN dispatch, PESEL, NIP, Luhn) plus debug twins that plant wrong weights or wrong parity. They all follow the same skeleton, and none of them is about 'remembering weights' — it is about knowing **where the weights come from** so you can re-derive them.

steps.title: Sanitise
steps.text: Strip the separators humans add: spaces and dashes (`'/[\s-]/'`). Checksums are defined on the bare digit string.

steps.title: Shape-check
steps.text: Exact length + digits-only, with `^` `$` anchors. `'/^[0-9]{11}$/'` for PESEL, `'/^[0-9]{9}[0-9X]$/'` for ISBN-10, etc. Wrong shape → `false`, immediately.

steps.title: Weighted sum
steps.text: Multiply each digit by its positional weight and add the products. The weights are the *only* thing that differs between algorithms.

steps.title: Derive the check digit and compare
steps.text: Compute what the last digit *should* be from the sum, then compare with the actual last digit. If they differ, the number is invalid.

payload.title: The universal skeleton
payload.intro: Every validator below is this skeleton with different weights. Debug a validator by checking each stage against a known-valid example — that is how the planted wrong-weight bugs in this module are found.

sections.title: Luhn: double every second digit from the right

payload.text: Used by card numbers. Count from the **rightmost** digit: double every second digit; if doubling makes it ≥ 10, subtract 9 (same as adding the two digits); sum everything; valid if the total ends in 0. 'From the right' is the whole difficulty — a left-to-right implementation only works for odd lengths, which is exactly the planted bug in the *'doubles the wrong digits for even-length numbers'* debug task.

steps.title: Write the digits with parity from the right
steps.text: For `79927398713` (11 digits) the rightmost digit `3` is NOT doubled, then alternately: the pattern from the left is *single, double, single, double…* because the length is odd.
steps.state:
digits:  7 9 9 2 7 3 9 8 7 1 3
pattern: s D s D s D s D s D s

steps.title: Apply double-and-subtract-9
steps.text: Doubled digits: `9→9` (18−9), `2→4`, `3→6`, `8→7` (16−9), `1→2`. Singles stay. Add every term:

steps.title: Total and verdict
steps.text: The running total is **70**, and `70 % 10 === 0` → valid.

payload.title: Reference — the parity is computed from the total length, not the loop index

payload.text: For the 16-digit `4417123456789113`, the rightmost digit is again not doubled, so from the left the pattern is **double, single, double, single…** — the opposite of the 11-digit case. A loop that doubles `$i % 2 === 1` only works for one parity; the reference above derives the parity from `$len - $i`, which is length-agnostic. Both numbers are valid Luhn numbers: `4417123456789113` doubles 4,1,1,3,5,7,9,1.
payload.title: Parity depends on the length, not on your mood

sections.title: ISBN-10 and ISBN-13: two generations, two moduli

steps.title: The check digit is 10 − (sum mod 11)
steps.text: `130 mod 11 = 9`, so the check digit is `(11 − 9) mod 11 = 2` — matching the last digit. A check digit of 10 is written as the letter `X`.

steps.title: Equivalent view: total must divide by 11
steps.text: Including the check digit (weight 1), the grand total is `132`, and `132 mod 11 = 0` → valid. Either formulation works.

steps.title: Alternating weights 1, 3, 1, 3… from the left
steps.text: `9780306406157`: digit × weight gives `9+21+8+0+3+0+6+12+0+18+1+15` before the check digit.

steps.title: Check digit makes the total a multiple of 10

payload.title: ISBN-10 reference — note the 'X' branch

sections.title: PESEL: a birth-date code with a mod-10 check

payload.text: PESEL is 11 digits: YYMMDD + a four-digit sequence number (with month offset for centuries) + one check digit. The check uses ten weights that **cycle 1, 3, 7, 9**: `1 3 7 9 1 3 7 9 1 3`. That cycle is the classic thing to get wrong — the debug task plants weight `2` at the start.

payload.title: PESEL 44051401359 — digit × weight, running total
payload.note: Check digit = (10 − (101 mod 10)) mod 10 = 9 — matches the last digit → valid. Digits: born 1944-05-14, sequence 013.

payload.text: `$check = (10 - ($sum % 10)) % 10;` — the outer `% 10` matters: when the sum already ends in 0, plain `10 − 0` would give 10, which is not a digit. The double mod makes the result 0..9.
payload.title: The double modulo is not a typo

steps.title: Check digit is sum mod 11 — unless it's 10
steps.text: `118 mod 11 = 8`, and the last digit is `8` → valid. NIP has no digit '10', so a check of 10 means the whole number is invalid (`return false`), not 'X' like ISBN-10.

payload.title: Four validators compared
rows: double every 2nd from the right, −9 if ≥ 10

payload.text: They are the same muscle with different weights — and each appears verbatim in Polish interview homework. Once you have written one correctly and **debugged it against a known-valid number**, the others are ten minutes each. That is the value of the debug twins in this module: they teach you to verify, not to hope.
payload.title: The four validators are one skill

lessons.title: Array mechanics: projection, sorting, grouping
lessons.summary: PHP's array functions each answer one precise question — project a column, sort by value, keep keys, deduplicate, flatten. Learn the comparator contract and PHP 8's stable sort, then rebuild the group / sort / dedup / paginate drills.

payload.text: Two quiz questions (array_column, uasort) plus five snippet tasks (group_by, sort_by_key, dedup_by_key, flatten, paginate_array) all test the same underlying skill: **knowing which built-in does what, and what it does to keys**. Interviewers watch whether you reach for the named function or hand-roll a loop.

sections.title: Sorting: what each function does to your keys

payload.text: PHP has four sorting families that look alike and behave very differently. The 'u' prefix means *user-defined comparison*, and 'a' means *associative (keys kept)*. Everything sorts **in place** and returns a `bool` — a classic slip is `$sorted = usort(...)` (you just assigned `true`).

payload.title: uasort keeps keys, usort does not

payload.text: All PHP sorts are **stable** since 8.0: elements the comparator declares equal keep their original relative order. That lets you sort by a secondary key first and a primary key second — the equal groups stay in secondary order. The dojo's `sort_by_key` task relies on stability for its tie-breaking.
payload.title: Equal elements keep their order

steps.title: Rows with a group key
steps.text: Start: `z (g=1)`, `a (g=1)`, `m (g=0)` — in that order.

steps.title: Stable sort by group only
steps.text: Group 0 first, then group 1 — and because the sort is stable, `z` still precedes `a` inside group 1 (their original order).

steps.title: Now sort each group by name
steps.text: A second, primary sort on the name of elements *within already-sorted groups* is what multi-key sorting needs. In `sort_by_key`, an explicit original-index tiebreaker makes the stability guarantee explicit even before PHP 8.
steps.state: grouped, then ordered inside each group

steps.title: array_column: the purpose-built tool
steps.text: `array_column($rows, 'id')` returns the `id` values in row order — one call, no closure. It is the quiz question's answer and the fastest option.

steps.title: The third argument re-indexes
steps.text: `array_column($rows, 'email', 'id')` keys the result by another column — instantly an id → email lookup map.

steps.title: Why NOT array_filter
steps.text: `array_filter($rows, fn($r) => $r['id'])` returns whole rows, and the callback is a **truthiness** test: a row with `id = 0` is dropped silently. Filtering is selection, not projection.

payload.title: Project a column without a loop
group_by — grouping is just keying an accumulator

steps.title: Keep the first row per key value
steps.text: Walk the rows; if the key value was already seen, skip — otherwise remember it (strictly!) and keep the row.

steps.title: Strict in_array is non-negotiable
steps.text: `in_array($v, $seen, true)` — without strict mode, the value `0` would collide with `'0'` and `false`, silently dropping valid rows. Same lesson as the comparison module, different disguise.

sections.title: Flattening is recursion wearing a disguise

payload.title: flatten — nested arrays, one level at a time

steps.title: Leaf or branch?
steps.text: For each element: if it is an array, it is a branch → recurse; otherwise it is a leaf → append.

steps.title: Trace one level
steps.text: `flatten([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])`: `1` appends, `[2,[3,4]]` recurses into `2` + `flatten([3,4])` = `[3,4]` → `[2,3,4]` spread in, `5` appends.

payload.text: `paginate_array` is the simplest of the family and the easiest to get wrong under time pressure: 1-based pages need `array_slice($items, ($page - 1) * $perPage, $perPage)`. The `- 1` is the whole task — page 1 must slice from index 0.

- `array_column($rows, 'id')` — *'projects one column out of rows'*.
- `uasort` vs `usort` — *'uasort keeps keys, usort reindexes'*.
- `array_filter` — *'keeps rows whose callback is truthy — it selects, it does not project'*.
- Sort functions — *'modify in place and return bool; stable since PHP 8'*.
- `array_map` — *'applies to every element, returns the same shape'*.
If you can fire these off, the array section of any interview is two minutes of easy points.
payload.title: Drill these until automatic

lessons.title: foreach by reference: the silent corruption
lessons.summary: After foreach ($arr as &$v), $v stays bound to the last element. Any later by-value loop over the same array silently overwrites that element. Learn the pointer mechanics and the one-line fix.

payload.text: This is the hardest quiz question in the module and the most 'trap-shaped' PHP behaviour you can be asked about, because it produces **no error, no notice** — just quietly wrong data. The dojo question asks for the cause and the fix; this lesson makes the mechanics visible.

In a **by-value** foreach, `$v` is a fresh copy of each element. In a **by-reference** foreach (`&$v`), `$v` is made to *alias* the current element's storage — and when the loop ends, `$v` is **still aliasing the last element**. Nothing resets it. If you later reuse `$v` in another loop over the same array, every assignment `$v = ...` writes straight into the array's last slot.

payload.title: The classic corruption, no unset
The array's state through the second loop

payload.html:
foreach ($arr as &$v)loop 1 ↓ $v ⇒ $arr[2]alias survives!
→
foreach ($arr as $v)loop 2 ↓ $v = $x writes into $arr[2]silent corruption
→
[1, 2, 2]wrong data, no error
payload.title: Where the alias goes after the first loop

steps.title: Break the alias immediately
steps.text: The line right after the by-reference loop: `unset($v);`. This removes the variable's alias — later loops get a normal copy again.

steps.title: Verify
steps.text: With `unset($v)`, the second loop behaves like any by-value loop and `$arr` stays `[1, 2, 3]`.

payload.title: unset($v) — no matter what, right after the loop

payload.text: Whenever you write `foreach ($arr as &$v)`, write `unset($v);` on the very next line **before writing the loop body**. The by-reference form is only needed when you genuinely mutate elements in place; for everything else prefer by-value with an indexed loop (`foreach ($arr as $k => $v)` + `$arr[$k] = ...`) which has no lingering alias at all.
payload.title: The habit that makes the bug impossible

payload.text: Interview follow-ups to expect: 'why does this only reproduce when a *second* loop follows?' (because the corruption needs a write through the stale alias) and 'does PHP 8 still do this?' (yes — it is semantics, not a version quirk).

lessons.title: Generators: why yield keeps memory flat
lessons.summary: A function containing yield returns a resumable Generator, not its values. Watch execution pause and resume between iterations, and understand why reading a million rows never allocates a million-row array.

payload.text: The generator quiz question is really three questions in one: what does the function **return**, when does its body **run**, and where do the values **live**. The mental model is a paused coroutine — the function keeps its own state between yields.

sections.title: A generator is a resumable function

payload.title: Execution interleaves with the consumer

steps.title: Calling the function runs nothing
steps.text: `steps()` returns a `Generator` object immediately — the body does not execute until the first iteration (the '[gen] starting' echo fires only inside the foreach).

steps.title: Each iteration = resume until next yield
steps.text: The consumer pulls one value, the generator runs up to the next `yield`, suspends, and keeps its local state for the next resume.

steps.title: A final return value is allowed
steps.text: `return $x;` (not `yield`) ends iteration and stores a value read afterwards with `$gen->getReturn()` — handy for a summary after yielding rows.

payload.title: Who runs when — generator vs consumer

payload.text: Building `range(1, 1_000_000)` materialises a million-element array in memory (tens of megabytes on PHP 8). A generator that `yield`s each integer holds **one** value plus its own state — a few hundred bytes no matter how long the sequence. Same for a big file or a database cursor: read one row, `yield` it, forget it.

payload.title: The classic use: streaming a file

steps.title: Yield from delegates to another generator
steps.text: `yield from $other;` forwards every value of another iterable/generator — compose pipelines without intermediate arrays.

steps.title: Generators are single-use
steps.text: A `Generator` can be iterated once; re-iterating yields nothing. Build a fresh one (call the function again) if you need two passes.

steps.title: Infinite sequences are fine
steps.text: Because generation is lazy, an unbounded sequence is safe — the consumer just `break`s when it has enough.

payload.text: When an interviewer asks about generators, they want to hear the *pain* they solve: memory-bound loops (huge CSV, export streams, SQL result sets) and composable lazy pipelines. The phrase that lands: **'a generator is a function that can pause — it produces values on demand instead of building the whole collection up front.'**
payload.title: One sentence for the interview
